shop:alley-18.koreaEvidence:
Cheonggyecheon Used Bookstore Stall

A green awning shades a compact secondhand bookstore in Seoul’s Pyeonghwa Market, where piles of books—ranging from textbooks to novels—are stacked on stools, tables, and the pavement. The wooden sign above the entrance proclaims “동신서림” and highlights its “50년전통,” while contact numbers and a website URL flank the name. Bundled volumes tied with string hint at the shop’s long history of serving students and collectors alike.

This stall is one of roughly twenty remaining shops on the Cheonggyecheon used bookstore street, which once boasted over two hundred vendors in the 1960s and 1970s. Recognized as a Seoul Future Heritage in 2013, the area has struggled against the rise of large bookstores and online retailers. Annual book festivals and pop‑up events aim to draw visitors back, but the narrow aisles and dense stacks of aging volumes remain a testament to the street’s enduring charm and cultural significance.

Through the glass windows, rows of colorful products are visible under bright interior lights, hinting at a well-stocked interior.

The scene captures the everyday charm of a local Seoul toy shop, with overhead power lines and neighboring buildings framing the urban environment. The combination of branded signage and neatly arranged merchandise conveys a lively retail atmosphere in a busy city district.

shop:alley-21.koreaEvidence:
풍년철물: Seoul’s Vintage Hardware Store

Nestled near the Dongmyo flea market in Seoul, 풍년철물 stands as a living relic of Changsin-dong’s past. Its hand-painted sign and striped awning welcome visitors to a densely packed storefront where coils of cable, chains, shovels, and various hardware items spill onto the sidewalk. A phone number, TEL 2235-2757, is prominently displayed beneath the shop’s name, reinforcing its decades-old presence in the neighborhood.

Inside and out, the shop offers a glimpse into traditional Korean ironmongery. Stacks of packaged tools and neatly coiled hoses contrast with the worn concrete pavement, while a lone customer seated nearby adds to the scene’s authenticity. 풍년철물’s enduring charm lies in its unchanging facade and the array of everyday metal goods that continue to serve both locals and visitors seeking a taste of Seoul’s industrial heritage.

OneLux Lighting Showroom in Euljiro

OneLux occupies a 60㎡ retail space in Seoul’s bustling Euljiro lighting district, where storefronts compete to showcase their fixtures. The store’s black exterior and dark green interior walls serve to amplify the glow of the pendant lights hung densely in the front display area. 

Designed by Seonsu Lee of JJSSBROS and completed in January 2018, the showroom merges two former rooms into one cohesive space. Visitors enter into a moody pendant display zone before moving into a brighter consultation and office area at the rear.

Gallery O'Clock Watch Repair Shop

Gallery O'Clock presents a sleek white storefront on a Seoul street, proudly displaying its long history since 1989. The signage highlights its expertise in luxury watch services, including Rolex, Cartier, Omega, and Seiko repairs. A glass door and window reveal a tidy interior with chairs and repair equipment, while a sandwich board outside advertises battery, band, and glass replacement services.

The shop specializes in comprehensive wristwatch maintenance—battery changes, band swaps, glass replacements, overhauls, and polishing—using genuine parts for high-end brands. Pricing starts at 10,000 KRW for standard watch battery replacements and 30,000 KRW for luxury models. Customer reviews commend the friendly service, affordable rates, and overall satisfaction, reflecting the shop’s reputation in Gireum-dong, Seongbuk-gu, Seoul.

A small neighborhood alteration shop in Sillim-dong, Gwanak-gu, Seoul, features a wooden facade and glass double doors. Bold yellow and red signage reads “A급 옷수선” with the phone number 010-2322-7732, while a smaller sign advertises “소담 옷방” and “수선전문.” A blue awning shades the entrance, and a bright sandwich board on the sidewalk repeats the shop’s name.

Inside, the shop specializes in a variety of clothing repairs—suit adjustments, leather and denim mending, zipper replacements, and school uniform alterations. Operating daily from 10:00 to 20:00 (closed Sundays), the business leverages 30 years of tailoring experience. Customers praise the owner’s meticulous work, quick turnaround, and reasonable pricing, with basic trouser hemming starting at 5,000 KRW and waist adjustments at 8,000 KRW.

Nestled on a quiet stretch of Tojeong‑ro in Seoul’s Hapjeong‑dong district, Acrobat presents a sleek wooden and brick façade topped by bold black lettering. A quaint analog film photography studio stands at a five-way intersection in Yeonhui-dong, Seoul.
